effects.log: Ten years late, the wedding feast. {npc} and the spouse eat it in their old wedding clothes.

events.text: {npc}, a baker, has caught a child stealing buns for the third time, and cannot bring {him}self to call the watch. {He} asks what you would do.

effects.log: A sick grandmother and an empty house. {npc} gives the child a bag of buns and a job.

choices.text: Put the child to work at the oven

effects.log: The child is good with the oven. {npc} is good with the child. The buns stop disappearing.

events.text: The bun thief has turned out to be the best baker {npc} has ever trained, and {npc} wants you to taste the child's first sweet bun.

choices.text: Taste it and give a verdict

ok.log: It is excellent. You say so. The child goes pink.

fail.log: It is a bit burnt. You say so. The child makes another one, perfect.

effects.log: You say nothing and eat three. The child understands that this is the highest praise.

events.text: {npc} is giving the bakery to the bun thief, and asks you to be witness to the paper.

effects.log: The paper says the bakery passes to the best baker in the street. Your name is underneath.

choices.text: Bring the grandmother from long ago a bun

effects.log: The grandmother is very old and very proud. {npc} says the circle is closed.

events.text: {npc}, the night watchman, has a fever and nobody to walk the rounds. {He} asks if you will carry the rattle and call the hours tonight.

effects.log: The third hour, all is well. The fourth hour, all is well. A cat disagrees.

choices.text: Wake the neighbours to share it

effects.log: Five neighbours, one rattle, five hours. The town has never been so well watched.

events.text: {npc} is well again, and has heard that on your rounds you caught a burglar. You did not. A cat knocked over a pot.

effects.log: {npc} laughs and says most of the burglars in {his} career were cats.
By midsummer you caught three burglars and a ghost. {npc} tells it best.

events.text: {npc} is retiring, and the town is looking for a new watchman, and {npc} has put your name forward.

choices.text: Take the rattle for a year

effects.log: A year of nights. You catch one real burglar. {npc} is prouder of that than of anything.
A tall, sleepless cousin of the baker. {npc} trains them, and the town sleeps well.

events.text: {npc}, a poor scholar, needs money for the journey to the capital exam, and has nothing to offer but {his} calligraphy.

effects.log: {npc} bows three times and leaves for the capital the next morning, writing a poem about you on the way.

ok.log: Six scrolls sold in a day. {npc} has enough for the road and a little over for ink.

fail.log: Two scrolls sold. Enough for half the road. {npc} walks the rest.

events.text: A letter from the capital: {npc} has passed. There is a poem about you in it, and the line about you is the best one.

choices.text: Write back with a poem of your own

ok.log: Your poem is very bad. {npc} frames it.

fail.log: Your poem is so bad {npc} reads it at a banquet for laughs, and toasts you.

choices.text: Write back with the news of home

effects.log: {npc} replies that the news of home is the only thing worth reading in the capital.

events.text: {npc} is a magistrate now, of a county near you, and comes in person to repay the old loan, with interest, and a scroll.

choices.text: Take the scroll, and not the money

effects.log: The scroll is the poem about you, written out fair. {npc} says the money was always yours. You put it toward a school.
You have dinner, and {npc} talks about being a magistrate, and you both agree it is mostly paperwork.

events.text: {npc} has dropped the washing paddle in the river, and with it a ring {he} had tied to the handle for safe keeping. The paddle is floating away.

choices.text: Run along the bank after it

ok.log: You catch it at the bend, ring and all. {npc} has run the whole way behind you.

fail.log: You fall in. The paddle floats to you. You come out with it, and a fish.

effects.log: Cold water and a good catch. The ring is still tied. {npc} dries you on the stones.

events.text: {npc} has tied a little bell to the paddle, so it can never be lost again, and the bell has frightened the ducks off the washing stones.

effects.log: Bread crusts and patience. The ducks return. They now come to the sound of the bell.
A smaller bell. The ducks are calm. {npc} says you are a philosopher of ducks.

events.text: {npc} gives you the ring from the paddle, wrapped in a leaf, and says it would have been in the sea if not for you.

effects.log: A plain silver ring. You wear it on a string. It brings you back to rivers.

choices.text: Give it back, tied to a better paddle

effects.log: A new paddle, with the ring set into the handle. {npc} never lets go of it.

events.text: The woodpile behind {npc}'s house has caught fire, and {npc} is throwing water on it with a teacup.

effects.log: The neighbours come running. Forty buckets. The fire is out. {npc} is still holding the teacup.

choices.text: Beat it out with wet sacks

ok.log: Smoke and heat, then it is out. Your eyebrows are shorter.

fail.log: The heat drives you back, then the neighbours arrive. The fire is out. Your hands sting for a week.

events.text: {npc} has bought a bucket for every house in the lane, painted red, and hung them all by the well, and wants you to name the lane's fire brigade.

effects.log: {npc} is outraged and then proud. The name sticks for fifty years.
{npc} protests. The buckets are painted with {npc}'s name anyway.

events.text: The Teacup Brigade is called to its first big fire, in the next lane, and {npc}, very old now, is leading it from a chair.

effects.log: Forty red buckets, the fire out in an hour. {npc} sits in the chair, holding the old teacup.

choices.text: Carry {npc} to safety and let the young run it

effects.log: {npc} shouts orders from your back. The young do it all. The fire is out.

events.text: Every morning for a week there is a folded letter tied to the plum tree outside your door. Every letter is a single line of poetry. Today {npc} is standing under the tree, pretending not to be.

choices.text: Write a line back and tie it to the tree

ok.log: You write a line. It is not good. The next morning there is a reply, correcting it, kindly.

fail.log: Your line is terrible. The next morning there is a reply: it says, this is terrible, and also, again.

effects.log: {npc} goes red to the ears and says good morning to the tree.

events.text: The plum letters have become a poem, a line a day for a month, half yours, half {npc}'s. Today {npc} brings the whole thing written out on one sheet.

effects.log: It is very bad and very good. A neighbour applauds from a window.
Tea, and then more tea. Neither of you mentions the poem, and it is all you talk about.

events.text: The plum tree is in flower again, a year on. {npc} is under it, holding a letter, and this one is not poetry.

effects.log: It says, plainly, what the poems were about. You tie your answer to the tree.
{npc} manages three words and gives up. You take it, and read it, and say yes to what it asks.

events.text: {npc} mends paper lanterns in the next street, and has mended yours four times this month. You have begun to suspect you are breaking it on purpose.

effects.log: {npc} laughs and admits {he} was mending it slowly on purpose, to see you come back.
{npc} mends it, and paints a small plum on it, and says that is to tell it from all the others.

events.text: The Lantern Festival. {npc} has made you a lantern of your own, shaped like a carp, and it has never been broken.

choices.text: Walk the river with it, together

effects.log: Two lanterns among thousands. You walk until they burn down.

choices.text: Write a riddle on it for {npc}

ok.log: {npc} solves it in a moment. The answer was {npc}'s name.

fail.log: {npc} cannot solve it. You tell the answer: {npc}'s name. {npc} is very quiet afterwards.

events.text: {npc}'s shop has been hit by a flood. The lanterns are ruined, and {npc} is sitting in the wet.

effects.log: A month of work. On the new shop's sign, {npc} paints a small plum. You both know what it means.

choices.text: Bring the carp lantern back to hang in the window

effects.log: The only dry lantern. {npc} hangs it in the window, and leans against you, and says nothing for a while.

events.text: {npc} has been watching you train in the yard for a week, and today asks, very formally, whether you would like a sparring partner.

ok.log: An even match. You are both too stubborn to stop. The sun goes down on a draw.

fail.log: {npc} wins easily, and offers you a hand up, and holds it a moment longer than needed.

effects.log: {npc} says it was your footwork. It was not your footwork.

events.text: You and {npc} have sparred every morning for a season. The yard's old caretaker has started selling tea to people who come to watch.

mem.note: put on a show with me

effects.log: The best fight the yard has seen in years, and it ends with you both laughing on the ground.
The river bank at dawn. No audience. {npc} lets you win once, and denies it forever.

events.text: {npc} lays down the practice sword in the middle of a bout and asks if you would rather stop fighting.

choices.text: Stop, and say what you have been meaning to

effects.log: The caretaker's customers applaud from the wall. Neither of you notices.

ok.log: You win, and then say it. {npc} says {he} let you win, and kisses your forehead, and you both know {he} did not.

fail.log: You lose, and say it from the ground. {npc} sits down next to you and says yes.

events.text: A sudden rain in the market, and {npc} offers to share an oiled-paper umbrella with you, though you are going the opposite way.

effects.log: You end up across town in the rain. Neither of you mentions how far it is.
You walk {npc} home under the umbrella. At the gate, {npc} hands it to you, so you can return it.

events.text: You have been returning {npc}'s umbrella for a month, and {npc} keeps lending it back, and the weather has been fine.

choices.text: Bring it back with a gift

effects.log: A packet of sweet osmanthus. {npc} lends you the umbrella again, at once, in sunshine.
{npc} has to come to your door for it. {He} stays for dinner.

events.text: A great storm, and {npc} is at your door with the umbrella, broken inside out, soaked to the skin, laughing.

effects.log: Tea by the stove. The broken umbrella dries in the corner. By morning you have decided some things.
Your hands get in each other's way all evening. The umbrella is never quite right again.

events.text: {npc}, the young herb doctor, has bandaged your cut hand and told you to come back in three days. It is a small cut. You have come back every day.

effects.log: The cut heals in a week. You keep coming. {npc} keeps finding something to check.

choices.text: Bring {npc} a herb you found on the hill

effects.log: It is a weed. {npc} plants it in the shop window anyway, where it thrives.

events.text: A fever in the district, and {npc} has not slept in a week, going house to house. {He} asks you to carry the basket.

effects.log: Fifty houses, a hundred bowls of bitter tea. At the end of it {npc} falls asleep on your shoulder.
{npc} protests and sleeps for six hours. You stand guard at the door with the basket.

events.text: {npc} has written you a prescription, in proper form, on proper paper, and handed it to you with a straight face.

effects.log: Take one herb doctor, daily, for life. You ask if there are side effects. {npc} says many.

ok.log: Your prescription is medically wrong and otherwise correct. {npc} frames it.

fail.log: Your prescription would kill a horse. {npc} laughs, and says yes anyway.

events.text: Picking season in the tea hills. {npc}, on the next row, has been picking twice as fast as you all morning, and now offers to show you the trick.

effects.log: Two leaves and a bud, a flick of the wrist. Your hand is in {npc}'s for the first lesson.

choices.text: Race {npc} to the end of the row

ok.log: You win, barely. {npc} demands a rematch, every day.

fail.log: {npc} wins by a basket. {npc} says the prize is that you carry both baskets down.

events.text: The end of picking season, and the hill holds a feast. {npc} has saved you a seat and a cup of the first tea.

mem.note: drank the first tea with me

effects.log: It is the best tea you have ever had. You suspect the company.
You are both terrible dancers, and the hill applauds that.

events.text: The tea season comes round again, and {npc} has bought a little terrace of {his} own, and wants to know if you will pick it with {him}.

effects.log: Two rows, one terrace. The first tea of it is yours to name.

choices.text: Plant a plum tree at the top of it

effects.log: The plum grows over the terrace. When it flowers, you both pick under it.

events.arc: The Letter Writer at the Gate
events.text: {npc} writes letters for people at the city gate, and has been writing yours home for a year. Today {he} asks if there is anyone you want to write to who is not at home.

effects.log: {npc} smiles and writes your letter home. At the end, {he} adds a line of {his} own, and asks you not to read it.

mem.note: had a letter written to me

effects.log: {npc} stares, and then laughs, and writes it, and reads it, and keeps it.

events.arc: The Letter Writer at the Gate
events.text: {npc}'s stall has been moved by the gate guards to a draughty corner, and the customers have stopped coming.

ok.log: The guards give in. {npc}'s stall is back by the gate, and the first letter of the day is to you.

fail.log: The guards will not move. You bring the customers to the corner yourself, a dozen a day.

effects.log: Bamboo and canvas. The corner is warm. {npc} writes you a poem about the windbreak.

events.arc: The Letter Writer at the Gate
events.text: {npc} hands you a letter sealed with red wax. On the outside, in {npc}'s best hand, is your name.

effects.log: It asks one question. You answer it at the stall, in person, and the line of customers applauds.

choices.text: Write the answer on the gate wall

ok.log: The whole city reads it. {npc} hides behind the stall and does not come out until evening.

fail.log: A guard corrects your spelling. The answer is still clear. {npc} comes out from behind the stall.

events.arc: The Boat on the Lotus Pond
events.text: {npc} has hired a little boat on the lotus pond, and has nobody to row it, and asks if you are strong.

effects.log: You row in a circle three times. {npc} laughs at every circle.
{npc} rows very well, which is a surprise to both of you. You sit and look at the lotus, and at {npc}.

events.arc: The Boat on the Lotus Pond
events.text: The lotus pond again, and {npc} has brought a basket of lotus seeds and a book of poems.

ok.log: You read well. A heron stops fishing to listen.

fail.log: You read badly. {npc} takes the book and reads beautifully, and gives it back.

effects.log: {npc} reads. You shell seeds. Neither of you notices that you have drifted into the reeds.

events.arc: The Boat on the Lotus Pond
events.text: The boat is stuck in the reeds, and the sun is going down, and {npc} says {he} does not mind in the least.

choices.text: Say you do not mind either

mem.note: stayed in the reeds with me

effects.log: The moon comes up. The lotus closes. You row back by the stars, in no hurry.

choices.text: Wade out and push the boat free

effects.log: You are muddy to the waist. {npc} pulls you into the boat and does not let go.

events.text: At the calligraphy class, {npc} sits beside you and keeps stealing your ink, saying {his} has gone dry. {His} has not gone dry.

effects.log: You share. Your characters improve. {npc}'s improve too, apparently.
The class becomes a war of ink. The teacher separates you, which is worse.

events.text: The class exhibition. {npc} has written only one scroll, and will not let you see it until the day.

effects.log: The scroll is your name, in {npc}'s best hand, enormous. The class murmurs.
You peek. You see your name. {npc} sees you peek, and turns crimson.

events.text: {npc} has asked the teacher to set the two of you a single scroll, to write together, one character each.

ok.log: The characters are uneven and the scroll is beautiful. It says: together.

fail.log: The scroll is a mess. It says together, more or less. You hang it anyway.

effects.log: {npc} chooses the words of a promise, and you write your half of it without hesitating.

events.text: A fan dancer in the travelling troupe, {npc}, loses a shoe in the crowd at the end of the show. You have it.

effects.log: {npc} hops over on one foot to thank you, and keeps hopping beside you all the way to the noodle stall.
Your joke is about shoes. {npc} laughs, and asks to hear another one at tomorrow's show.

events.text: The troupe stays a month in town, and {npc} has been dancing better than ever, and says it is because you are always in the front row.

effects.log: Every night. The troupe gives you a stool. {npc} dances the last dance toward you.

ok.log: You learn the first part. You perform it badly on the last night, and {npc} joins you.

fail.log: You fall over the fan. {npc} helps you up, laughing, in front of everyone.

events.text: The troupe is leaving. {npc} stands at the cart, with one shoe in {his} hand, the same shoe, and asks if you will keep it.

choices.text: Keep the shoe, and ask {npc} to stay

effects.log: {npc} stays. The troupe leaves one dancer short. The shoe sits on your shelf.
You take the road with the troupe for a season, carrying the costumes. You see the whole country, and mostly {npc}.

events.text: You and {npc} reach the well at the same moment every dawn. It has happened twelve days running. Today {npc} has brought a second bucket, for you.

effects.log: You draw water together. {npc} talks about the weather as if it were important.
You carry both. {npc} walks beside you with nothing, and does not stop smiling.

events.text: The neighbours have noticed the well. Every dawn now there are three old people on a bench, watching, eating seeds.

effects.log: The old people wave back. One gives a thumbs up. {npc} hides behind the bucket.
A well on the far side of town. The old people find it in a week.

events.text: Midsummer. {npc} is at the well and has drawn no water at all, and says {he} has something to say before the old people arrive.

effects.log: You say it. {npc} laughs with relief. The old people arrive and applaud, mid-seed.
{npc} says it, all in one breath. You say yes before the breath is over.

events.text: At the night market, {npc} is trying to win a paper fish at a ring-toss stall and has spent a fortune and won nothing.

ok.log: First throw. {npc} holds the paper fish like a trophy.

fail.log: You miss too. You both laugh at the stall-keeper, who is getting rich.

choices.text: Buy {npc} a fish from the next stall (1 tael)

effects.log: It is a better fish. {npc} says it does not count, and keeps it.

events.text: The night market again. {npc} has been practising ring toss in {his} yard for a month, and wants to win you something this time.

mem.note: let me win something for you

effects.log: Eleventh throw: a paper tiger. {npc} gives it to you with great ceremony.
Two rings, one peg. You win a paper pair of mandarin ducks. The stall-keeper winks.

events.text: {npc} has kept every paper prize, and they hang over {his} window: fish, tiger, ducks. {He} adds one more in front of you: a paper ring.

effects.log: You wear it until it falls apart. {npc} makes another, and another.
{npc} looks at it, and at you, and at the paper one, and laughs and cries at once.

events.text: A lost dog follows you home from the market. The next morning {npc} turns up: the dog is {his}, and apparently it prefers your house.

effects.log: {npc} takes the dog home. That night, the dog is back. So, the next morning, is {npc}.

choices.text: Invite {npc} in while the dog decides

effects.log: The dog decides to sleep across both your feet. You have tea. It takes the dog a long time to decide.

events.text: The dog now walks between your house and {npc}'s every day, and {npc} has started walking with it.

effects.log: Three of you on the river path. The dog leads. Nobody hurries.

choices.text: Build the dog a kennel halfway between

effects.log: A kennel under the bridge, halfway. The dog never uses it. You and {npc} sit there often.

events.text: The dog is old now, and {npc} says it is only fair that it should live in one house. {He} looks at you and does not say which.

choices.text: Say it should live wherever {npc} lives

mem.note: heard where the dog should live

effects.log: {npc} says then you had better live there too. The dog agrees.

choices.text: Say the dog has always known

effects.log: The dog lies across both your feet. That settles it.

events.text: Your rival {npc} has claimed the best hill for kite-flying and charges the other children one sweet to use it.

ok.log: You fly from the hill. {npc} cannot stop you, and pretends it was free that day.

fail.log: {npc} and two friends block the path. You fly from the ditch. Your kite goes higher anyway.

effects.log: {npc} is confused by your good mood, and eats the sweet suspiciously.

events.text: A storm has torn {npc}'s kite to pieces, and {npc} is sitting on the hill with the sticks, not crying.

effects.log: You mend it together. It flies crooked. {npc} pretends it is better that way.

mem.note: flew yours in front of me

effects.log: {npc} watches your kite with open envy, and builds a better one that winter.

events.text: You are both too old for kites, and both on the hill anyway, the day of the spring wind.

effects.log: Two kites, one hill, no charge. {npc} says you still fly like a duck.

ok.log: You win, barely. {npc} says the hill was always yours, and does not mean it.

fail.log: {npc} wins and lies on the grass at the top, gloating, kite forgotten.

events.text: {npc} has caught a fish the length of an arm and is carrying it round the village. Everyone says nobody will ever catch a bigger one.

choices.text: Fish all day for a bigger one

ok.log: At dusk, an arm and a hand. The village forgets {npc}'s fish. {npc} does not forget yours.

fail.log: Seven small fish. {npc} counts them aloud, slowly.

effects.log: {npc} tells you, proudly, the wrong place. You know it is the wrong place. You both know.

events.text: The village holds a fishing contest, and the two of you are in the last boats on the lake.

ok.log: You win by one carp. {npc} shakes your hand so hard it hurts.

fail.log: {npc} wins. You clap. {npc} does not know what to do with the clapping.

effects.log: Two boats tied together. You both catch nothing and both enjoy it.

events.text: {npc} has a fish stall now, and a sign over it says: the biggest fish in the county. Below, smaller: except one.

choices.text: Buy a fish and ask about the sign

effects.log: {npc} says the sign is honest. You are the one. You laugh, and so does {npc}, at last.

ok.log: {npc} looks at it a long time and changes the sign to: except two.

fail.log: Yours is smaller. {npc} hangs it beside the sign as a warning to others.

events.text: The county exam, and of all the hundreds of cells in the hall, your rival {npc} has the one next to yours. You can hear {npc} grinding ink, smugly.

choices.text: Write the best essay of your life

ok.log: You place above {npc}. {npc} reads your essay on the wall twice, frowning.

fail.log: {npc} places above you, and reads your essay on the wall, and says it was not bad.

choices.text: Pass {npc} your spare ink when it runs out

effects.log: {npc}'s ink runs out halfway. Yours comes under the partition. Neither of you mentions it afterwards.

events.text: {npc} has failed a higher exam and is sitting alone on the steps of the hall, and you have come out of it too.

mem.note: sat with me after the exam

effects.log: You say nothing. Then you both say how bad the third question was, and laugh.
You walk past. {npc} sees. Next year, {npc} studies twice as hard.

events.text: You are both on the examining board for the county, and the two of you must agree on the top paper.

choices.text: Argue all night for your choice

ok.log: {npc} gives in at dawn. It was the right paper. {npc} says so first.

fail.log: {npc} wins. It was the right paper. You say so first.

choices.text: Choose the paper neither of you would have picked

effects.log: A strange, honest essay from a poor village. You both agree. It is the first time.

events.text: Your rival {npc} has set up a stall right beside yours in the market, selling the same thing, a copper cheaper.

ok.log: You win the customers back. {npc} drops another copper. You both sell at a loss for a week.

fail.log: {npc} wins the price war. You learn something about business.

effects.log: Mornings yours, afternoons {npc}'s. Both stalls do better. Neither of you will say so.

events.text: A tax collector is squeezing the whole market, and {npc} is the first to stand up to the collector, alone.

effects.log: Two of you, then ten, then the whole market. The collector leaves. {npc} looks at you as if seeing you for the first time.
{npc} is fined. You are not. {npc} does not forget.

events.text: {npc}'s stall has burned down in the night. Your stall is untouched, right beside it.

effects.log: Two sellers at one stall. The customers think it is a new business. In a way it is.
{npc} rebuilds, and pays you back in a year, to the copper, and still undercuts you by one.

events.text: You come to the training yard at dawn to be the first, and your rival {npc} is already there. Tomorrow you come earlier. So does {npc}.

choices.text: Come in the middle of the night

ok.log: You win, once. {npc} sleeps in the yard the next night.

fail.log: {npc} is there, asleep on the bench. You train in silence beside the snoring.

effects.log: Neither of you says a word for a month. Both of you get much better.

events.text: {npc} has hurt a knee and cannot train for a season, and comes to the yard anyway, at dawn, to watch you.

choices.text: Train as if {npc} were still racing you

effects.log: You train harder than ever. {npc} shouts corrections from the bench, unfairly.
{npc} is a terrible patient and a very good coach.

events.text: Twenty years of dawns. The yard is to be sold, and you and {npc} are the last two who still come.

effects.log: You paid 5 taels each. The yard is yours, both. You still race to be first.

ok.log: You win the last bout. {npc} laughs and says it took twenty years.

fail.log: {npc} wins the last bout. You laugh and say it took twenty years.

events.text: The magistrate is looking for someone to paint the new temple gate. You and your rival {npc} both submit a design. Both of you are told to come back with a better one.

ok.log: Your design wins. {npc} studies it, frowning, and then nods once.

fail.log: {npc} wins. You see the gate every day. It is very good. You hate it.

effects.log: Two styles on one gate, one each side. People argue about which side is better for years.

events.text: {npc} has been hired to paint a lord's hall, and has fallen sick in the middle of it. The lord is impatient.

ok.log: Nobody can tell where {npc} stopped and you began. Except {npc}, who can, and says nothing.

fail.log: Everyone can tell. The lord likes your half better. {npc} is mortified and grateful.

effects.log: The lord waits, angrily. {npc} finishes it, better than before.

events.text: You are both old painters now, and the magistrate wants the temple gate repainted. There is only budget for one.

mem.note: painted the gate with me again

effects.log: The same two sides, forty years on. People still argue. You both enjoy it.
{npc} paints both sides, and leaves one small corner in your style, as a signature.

events.text: Both of you have come to the same sect's entrance test, and your rival {npc} is in line just in front of you, already looking back.

choices.text: Pass first, and wait at the gate

ok.log: You pass. {npc} passes after. {npc} walks past you at the gate without a word.

fail.log: {npc} passes. You fail the first time, and pass the second. {npc} waits at the gate, smirking.

effects.log: {npc} looks for the trap. There is no trap. {npc} passes, and so do you.

events.text: The two of you are paired for a mission into the mountains. The elders say it is to teach you both something.

effects.log: You argue the whole way and complete it perfectly. The elders smile.

ok.log: You finish first, alone. The elders are not pleased. Neither, much, is {npc}.

fail.log: {npc} finishes first. You are both scolded for splitting up.

events.text: {npc} is to be tested for promotion, and the elders ask you to be the opponent.

ok.log: You fight hard. {npc} wins, just, and is promoted, and thanks you for not holding back.

fail.log: You fight hard. You win, just. {npc} is not promoted, and thanks you anyway, because it was fair.

choices.text: Refuse, and say {npc} needs no test

effects.log: The elders promote {npc} on your word. {npc} does not know whether to be grateful or furious, and is both.

events.text: On a narrow plank bridge over a gorge you meet your rival {npc}, coming the other way. Neither of you will step back.

ok.log: {npc} steps back. Then you both have to laugh at how long it took.

fail.log: You step back, eventually. {npc} crosses, nose in the air, and slips on the last plank.

effects.log: {npc} crosses, confused. Halfway, {npc} turns and bows back.

events.text: The plank bridge has collapsed in a storm, and {npc} is on the far side with an injured traveller.

ok.log: You throw the rope; {npc} catches it. Together you bring the traveller over.

fail.log: Three tries. On the fourth, it holds. {npc} grabs your arm at the end and does not let go for a moment.

effects.log: The woodcutters have a ladder. {npc} and the traveller are brought over. {npc} thanks you, awkwardly.

events.text: A stone bridge is to be built over the gorge. The county asks for two names to carve on it, and it is yours and {npc}'s.

effects.log: Two names on one stone. Which is first depends on which side you cross from. That was {npc}'s idea.
{npc} protests and insists yours goes first. The stonemason carves them side by side, to stop the argument.

events.text: The teahouse holds a singing evening. Your rival {npc} sings first, and the teahouse goes quiet. You are next.

ok.log: The teahouse goes quieter. {npc} stares into a teacup.

fail.log: You crack on the high note. {npc} applauds very loudly, which is worse.

effects.log: You join {npc}'s song. {npc} is furious for one line, and then sings with you. It is the best song of the night.

events.text: {npc} has lost {his} voice before the most important evening of the year, and has come, hoarse, to ask you to sing in {his} place.

ok.log: You sing it the way {npc} would have. The teahouse knows. {npc} wipes {his} eyes at the back.

fail.log: You sing it badly, but in {npc}'s honour. The teahouse cheers the gesture.

effects.log: You sing well. {npc} is quiet at the back, and comes the next year with a voice better than ever.

events.text: The two of you are old voices now, and the teahouse wants a last duet.

effects.log: Your voices are thinner, and fit better than they ever did. The teahouse sings the chorus.
{npc} sings, and looks at you at the end of every verse.

events.text: Your rival {npc} has made you promise, before witnesses, that whoever reaches the next realm of cultivation first will climb the old pine and ring the temple bell from its top.

effects.log: You shake. The witnesses cheer. The temple monks are not consulted.

choices.text: Make it the bell on the roof instead

effects.log: The terms are argued for an hour. It is the roof. The monks are still not consulted.

events.text: Word has come: one of you has broken through first. It is {npc}, by a month.

choices.text: Stand under the pine and watch {npc} climb

effects.log: {npc} climbs, rings, falls into a bush, and is triumphant. The monks chase you both off.
{npc} climbs anyway. The monks catch {npc} at the bottom. You negotiate the release.

events.text: Years on, the monks have hung a small bell on the old pine, low down, with a plaque: for promises.

effects.log: A small, clear note. {npc} says it is the only bell either of you could reach now.

choices.text: Make a new promise, before the old witnesses

effects.log: Whoever lives longer rings it for the other. You both shake on it.

events.text: On the dry road you fall in with a salt caravan. Its master, {npc}, a weathered trader with a lantern on a pole, offers you a place by the fire if you will stand a watch.

effects.log: A long cold night, nothing but stars and one curious fox. At dawn {npc} gives you a lump of salt the size of a fist, for luck.

choices.text: Tell stories at the fire instead

effects.log: The muleteers laugh until midnight. {npc} says you are hired as the caravan's liar, unpaid.

events.text: The salt caravan comes through your town. {npc} has lost two muleteers to a fever and is a week behind.

choices.text: Walk with the caravan to the next town

effects.log: Ten days of dust and mules. You learn to load a camel. {npc} pays you in salt and gossip.

choices.text: Find two hands in the market

effects.log: Two cousins of the baker, eager and useless. {npc} says they will learn. They do.

events.text: A last salt caravan. {npc} is selling the camels and stopping the road, and wants you at the last fire.

effects.log: Every muleteer who ever walked with {npc} is there. They tell the stories you told, much improved.

choices.text: Take the lantern on the pole

effects.log: {npc} hands you the lantern. You hang it by your door, and travellers knock to ask the way.

events.text: Snow on the high pass, and you find a stone hut with a fire laid and a pot of rice and a note: eat, and leave the hut as you found it.

effects.log: You sleep warm. In the morning you split twice the wood you burned and leave a note of your own.
You leave before dawn. The snow closes behind you. You never forget that pot of rice.

events.text: Back over the high pass. The hut's door is broken and the woodpile is gone, and nobody has left rice.

choices.text: Mend the door and stock the woodpile

effects.log: A whole day of work. You leave rice and a note. Eat, and leave the hut as you found it.

choices.text: Leave a little rice and go

effects.log: It is not much. The next traveller will find it, and that is the point.

events.text: Snow again, the pass again, and in the hut a frozen traveller who has not found the rice.

choices.text: Light the fire and cook the rice

effects.log: The traveller lives. In the spring a letter reaches you, care of the hut, from a family of six.

choices.text: Carry the traveller down the pass

ok.log: A long night, but the village at the bottom takes the traveller in. They name the hut after you.

fail.log: You are both half frozen at the bottom, but alive. The village takes you both in.

events.text: A travelling physician, {npc}, is sitting by the road with a twisted ankle and a box of medicines too heavy to carry now.

choices.text: Carry the box to the next town

effects.log: A heavy box and a cheerful patient. {npc} teaches you the names of every drawer on the way.

ok.log: A good splint. {npc} approves of your knots and corrects your angle.

fail.log: A bad splint. {npc} redoes it while explaining what you did wrong, kindly.

events.text: {npc}'s ankle is long healed, and {npc} has come to your town, where a cough is going round, and wants an assistant.

effects.log: A hundred patients. You learn more than in a year of books. {npc} gives you a drawer of your own.

choices.text: Find {npc} a room near the market

effects.log: A room above a noodle shop. The queue for {npc} goes round the block.

events.text: {npc} is retiring from the road, and has brought you the box of medicines, with every drawer relabelled in big characters.

effects.log: Forty drawers. You use them for years. Every drawer still has {npc}'s writing on it.

choices.text: Give the box to the town's young doctor

mem.note: gave my box to the young doctor

effects.log: The young doctor weeps. {npc} gives a lecture on the drawers that lasts all afternoon.

events.text: Behind a broken wall in the hills you find a garden gone wild: peonies taller than you, a pond full of frogs, a stone bench carved with two names.

effects.log: You sit on the bench. The frogs sing. Whoever the two names were, they chose well.
You plant it by your door. It flowers the next spring, enormous and red.

events.text: The garden again. Someone else has found it: the bench is cleared, the pond is clean, and there is a bowl of rice on the bench.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of your own

effects.log: The next time, there is a note in the bowl. It says: thank you. Nothing else.

ok.log: An old couple with a broom. It was their parents' garden. They give you peony seeds.

fail.log: Nobody comes. You weed the peonies for an afternoon, and that is a good afternoon.

events.text: The garden in spring. The peonies have spread down the hill, and the village below has started calling it the Garden of the Two Names.

choices.text: Carve your own name on the bench

effects.log: A third name, very small. You hope the other two do not mind.

choices.text: Bring the village children to see it

effects.log: Twenty children and a pond of frogs. The garden is loved again.

events.text: On the river ferry, an old scholar, {npc}, and a young boatman are arguing whether a fish knows it is wet. They turn to you to decide.

effects.log: The boatman sulks. {npc} gives you a reading list.
{npc} is outraged and delighted, and argues with you until the far bank.

events.text: The same ferry, the same {npc}, and a new question: if you cross the same river twice, is it the same river?

choices.text: Say it is the same river

effects.log: {npc} says it is not, and the boatman says it is the same fare. Everyone is happy.

ok.log: Cold, and different, you report. {npc} writes it down.

fail.log: The current takes you downstream. {npc} writes: it is a stronger river than it was.

events.text: {npc} has written a book of the ferry arguments. You are in it, under the name The Passenger Who Jumped.

effects.log: The book is very good. Your chapter is the funniest. {npc} signs it.

choices.text: Ask to write the last chapter

ok.log: You write about whether a book knows it is read. {npc} says it is the best chapter and is jealous.

fail.log: Your chapter is muddled. {npc} keeps it as an appendix.

events.text: A tiny shrine in the woods, no higher than your knee, with a little stone fox and a dish of old rice. The dish is empty.

effects.log: You leave a dumpling. When you look back, the dish is empty and there is nothing on the path.
You clear the moss. The fox's stone face looks pleased, though stone faces do not change.

events.text: You lose your purse on the road through the woods. The next morning, it is on the fox shrine, every coin in it.

effects.log: You leave a coin. It is gone in the morning. So is the dumpling you left beside it.
You leave the purse. A year later the woods' poorest farm finds a purse in its rice bin.

events.text: A fox crosses your path in the woods, carrying something. It drops it at your feet: a small stone fox, the twin of the one at the shrine.

effects.log: It sits on your shelf. Your house is never robbed, never burns, and is often visited by foxes.

choices.text: Put it beside the other at the shrine

effects.log: Two stone foxes side by side. The dish is full every time you pass.

events.arc: The Novice Who Lost the Way
events.text: A young temple novice, {npc}, is standing at a crossroads in the hills with a map upside down, too proud to ask, and clearly lost.

choices.text: Turn the map the right way

effects.log: {npc} thanks you with great dignity. The temple is the other way. {npc} goes the other way.
A two-day walk. {npc} talks the whole way about being lost, as a spiritual matter.

events.arc: The Novice Who Lost the Way
events.text: {npc} is the temple's guest master now, and has been put in charge of travellers, and keeps getting them lost.

choices.text: Draw the temple a proper map

effects.log: A map on a board by the gate. Nobody is lost again. {npc} is relieved and slightly sad.
Twelve signposts. {npc} writes a verse on each. The verses are about being lost.

events.arc: The Novice Who Lost the Way
events.text: {npc} is head of the temple now, and has never quite learned to read a map, and asks you to guide the temple's pilgrims to the high shrine this year.

effects.log: Two hundred pilgrims, one road. Nobody is lost. {npc} brings up the rear and gets lost once, briefly.

choices.text: Teach {npc} to read the map at last

effects.log: A whole afternoon. {npc} learns. Then holds it upside down at the door, out of habit.

events.text: The inn at the crossroads has a rule: at midnight every guest must tell a story. The innkeeper, {npc}, writes the best one on the wall.

ok.log: Your story goes on the wall. A guest refuses to sleep. {npc} is delighted.

fail.log: A muddled story. {npc} writes your name in small characters, for effort.

choices.text: Tell the truth about your life

effects.log: The inn goes quiet. {npc} writes it on the wall without a word.

events.text: The inn again, and {npc} has run out of wall. The new rule: whoever tells the best story paints the new wall.

choices.text: Paint a dragon round the stories

effects.log: The dragon is lopsided and the stories fit in its coils. {npc} names it after you.

ok.log: You win. You paint the wall the colour of plums. Guests talk about it for years.

fail.log: A peddler wins and paints the wall with fish. It is very good.

events.text: {npc} is retiring, and the inn is to close, and {npc} has asked every guest whose story is on the wall to come back for one last midnight.

choices.text: Come back and tell the last story

effects.log: You tell the story of the inn. {npc} writes it on the door, as there is no more wall.

choices.text: Copy the walls into a book

effects.log: Three hundred stories. {npc} reads the book every evening in the new house.

events.arc: The Flute in the Bamboo Grove
events.text: Deep in a bamboo grove the wind is playing a note, over and over. You find the cause: a stalk with a hole bored in it, by a beetle or by somebody.

choices.text: Cut the stalk into a flute

effects.log: Your flute plays three notes. The grove plays the same three back.
You sit and listen for an hour. You come away calmer than you went in.

events.arc: The Flute in the Bamboo Grove
events.text: You have been playing the grove flute for two years. The three notes have become a tune, and children follow you down the road.

effects.log: Six children with six flutes. The village is never quiet again.

choices.text: Go back and listen to the grove

effects.log: The grove plays a fourth note now. You learn it. It changes everything.

events.arc: The Flute in the Bamboo Grove
events.text: A traveller stops you on the road: the tune you are playing, the traveller says, is from a song that was lost two hundred years ago. You only know four notes of it.

choices.text: Go back to the grove for more

ok.log: The grove has more holes now. The beetle, or somebody, has been busy. You learn eleven notes.

fail.log: The grove is quiet. Four notes are what you have. You play them for the traveller.

choices.text: Teach the traveller your four notes

effects.log: The traveller writes them down and weeps. Four notes is more than anyone had.

events.text: In an abandoned village you find a well with coins in it, hundreds of years of them, glinting far down. The rope has rotted.

effects.log: You drop a coin. It takes a long time to land. You do not tell anyone what you wished.

ok.log: Old coins, a few silver. You climb out with your pockets full and an uneasy feeling.

fail.log: The rope breaks halfway. You climb out by the stones, scraped and empty-handed.

events.text: The abandoned village is being resettled by refugees from a flood, and they need the well, and the well is full of coins.

choices.text: Help clear the well for them

effects.log: You haul out coins and silt all week. The refugees use the coins to buy seed rice.

choices.text: Tell them to keep the coins in it

effects.log: They keep it as a wishing well and dig another. Both wells give sweet water.

events.text: The resettled village has grown into a town, and the old well is in the middle of the market, and everyone throws a coin in on their wedding day.

effects.log: The coin takes a long time to land, as always. Whatever you wished last time, you wish it again.

choices.text: Tell the town how it was when it was empty

effects.log: You tell it in the teahouse. Children listen, wide-eyed. The old well has a story now.

events.text: On the sea rocks an old fisher, {npc}, catches crabs with a bit of string and a stone, and has caught nine to your none.

effects.log: The trick is patience. {npc} says it in a way that makes it sound like a secret.

choices.text: Promise a dinner you can catch ten

ok.log: Ten crabs by sunset. {npc} cooks them all, and the dinner is yours.

fail.log: Two crabs by sunset. You cook dinner for {npc}, who eats it with great satisfaction.

events.text: A storm has smashed the rock pools, and {npc}'s favourite fishing rock is underwater. {npc} is sitting on the shore, sulking.

effects.log: A good flat rock round the point. {npc} catches eleven crabs on it and says the old one was better.
A day of hauling stones. The pool fills at high tide and keeps the crabs. {npc} calls it cheating, and uses it.

events.text: {npc} is too old for the rocks, and asks you to catch nine crabs, with string and a stone, and bring them to the hut.

ok.log: Nine by noon. {npc} cooks them, and says you have the trick at last.

fail.log: Four. {npc} says four is the number of a good student and cooks them anyway.

effects.log: {npc} catches one crab, slowly, and holds it up to you like a prize.

events.text: Under a stone bridge on the road, a dozen children are learning their characters from a teacher who writes in the mud with a stick. The teacher looks up, hopeful, at your brush case.

choices.text: Lend the teacher your brush and buy paper (1 tael)

effects.log: You paid 1 tael in paper. The children write their names on real paper for the first time. They keep the paper.
You teach the character for river. The children write it in the mud, then in the river.

events.text: The school under the bridge has grown to thirty children, and the bridge leaks.

effects.log: A shed of reeds. Thirty children, one dry corner each. The teacher writes your name over the door.

choices.text: Find the school a room in town

ok.log: A merchant gives a back room. The school moves in, and the children miss the bridge.

fail.log: No room is found. The children stay under the bridge. They like it.

events.text: A child from the school under the bridge has passed the county exam, the first from the river villages, and wants to thank you.

effects.log: The child says you taught the character for river, and it was the first character they ever learned.

choices.text: Give the child your old brush

effects.log: The child takes the brush, very carefully, and bows. The teacher, older now, is weeping.

events.text: On the road a mule follows you for a mile, then a young muleteer, {npc}, comes running after it, shouting that you have stolen it.

choices.text: Hand the mule back and laugh

effects.log: {npc} apologises, very red. The mule follows you again. {npc} follows the mule.
The mule walks to {npc}, nudges {npc}, then comes back to you. Nobody knows what that means.

events.text: {npc} and the mule turn up at your door: the mule has walked fifty miles to find you, and {npc} has given up.

effects.log: The mule is yours. It is perfectly happy. {npc} visits it every month.
{npc} works for you now. The mule works for nobody. Everyone is happy.

events.text: The mule is very old now, and {npc} has come to say goodbye to it, and has brought it a carrot every day for a week.

choices.text: Let {npc} lead it to the river once more

effects.log: The old mule walks to the river with {npc}, then turns round and comes home to you.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and the mule in the yard

mem.note: sat with me and the mule

effects.log: The mule eats the carrots. {npc} tells the story of the mile on the road, and you both laugh.

events.text: A temple clings to the cliff above the river, reached by a path of iron chains. The monk at the bottom says one pilgrim in ten turns back.

ok.log: You reach the top, shaking. The view takes the shaking away.

fail.log: Halfway, you turn back. The monk at the bottom says you are the one in ten, and gives you tea.

effects.log: The monk tells you stories of pilgrims who did not wait. You decide to wait.

events.text: Back at the cliff temple. A pilgrim halfway up the chains has frozen in fear.

choices.text: Climb up and talk them down

ok.log: You talk about noodles the whole way down. The pilgrim laughs and moves, step by step.

fail.log: You get halfway and freeze too. Together, talking about noodles, you both get down.

effects.log: The monks have a basket on a rope for this. The pilgrim is lowered, mortified and safe.

events.text: The cliff temple's chains have rusted, and the monks are raising money for new ones.

choices.text: Give money for one chain (3 taels)

effects.log: A link of the new chain has your name on it. You climb it the next spring.

choices.text: Climb the old chains once more before they go

ok.log: You reach the top. The view is the same. You are not.

fail.log: Halfway, and you come down. The monk says some views are better remembered.

events.text: A downpour on the mountain road, and the only shelter is a covered bridge, already crowded. A traveller, {npc}, makes room for you on the bench.

choices.text: Sit and share your rice cakes

effects.log: The rain goes on for hours. By the end the whole bridge is sharing everything.

choices.text: Play a game of stones with {npc}

effects.log: A board scratched on the plank. You play until the rain stops, and keep playing.

events.text: The covered bridge again, in the rain again, and {npc} is there again, on the same bench.

choices.text: Sit down and pick up where you left off

effects.log: The board is still scratched on the plank. You finish the game from memory.

choices.text: Ask what {npc} has done these years

effects.log: A long story, and a good one. The rain is not long enough for it.

events.text: The covered bridge is old and leaking. You and {npc} have agreed by letter to meet there and mend the roof.

effects.log: New tiles and old jokes. The next traveller who shelters there will be dry.

choices.text: Carve your names on the bench

effects.log: Two names on the bench where you met. The rain starts again, and you both sit down.

events.text: Under a tall tree you find a nest knocked down by the wind, with one egg still whole in it.

choices.text: Put it back in the tree

ok.log: You climb with the nest in your teeth. The mother bird screams at you all the way, then settles on it.

fail.log: You get it most of the way up and slip. The nest stays on a low branch. The mother bird finds it.

choices.text: Keep the egg warm in your shirt

effects.log: You walk around for three days very carefully. Then it hatches, on your chest, into a small, furious bird.

events.text: A bird keeps landing on your windowsill and staring at you. You are fairly sure it is the one from the nest.

effects.log: It eats from your hand. The neighbours think you are a sorcerer.

choices.text: Teach it to sit on your shoulder

ok.log: It sits there for a whole morning. The village children are deeply jealous.

fail.log: It sits on your head instead, and will not get off.

events.text: The bird has a nest of its own now, on your roof, and four eggs in it.

choices.text: Guard the nest from the cat

effects.log: A month of guarding. Four birds fly from your roof.
You watch from the yard every morning. When they fly, you feel you did something.

events.text: At the river an old fisher, {npc}, is skipping stones, and each stone jumps eleven times. {npc} says {he} is the stone-skipping champion of the river, and has been for fifty years.

ok.log: Your stone jumps four times. {npc} declares you an heir of the river.

fail.log: Your stone sinks. {npc} laughs and teaches you to choose flat ones.

effects.log: Flat stone, low arm, a flick. {npc} shows you a hundred times.

events.text: {npc} has found you the perfect skipping stone, flat as a coin, and says it has waited at the bottom of the river for you for a thousand years.

ok.log: Nine jumps. {npc} is speechless, then shouts for a long time.

fail.log: Five jumps. {npc} says a thousand years is not long enough for some stones.

effects.log: It stays in your pocket for years, flat and cool.

events.text: {npc} is too old for the riverbank, and sends word that the river needs a new champion.

choices.text: Skip twelve times and be crowned

ok.log: Twelve. The river children crown you with reeds. {npc} hears of it and laughs from bed.

fail.log: Seven. The river children crown you anyway, out of respect for {npc}.

choices.text: Carry {npc} to the river for one last stone

effects.log: {npc}'s last stone jumps eleven times. Of course it does.

events.text: Two ant hills in the yard are at war, black ants against red. You lie on your stomach and watch for an hour.

effects.log: You move a twig. The black ants win a great battle. You feel like a general.

choices.text: Make peace with a lump of sugar

effects.log: A lump of sugar between the hills. Both armies stop to eat it. Peace, for an afternoon.

events.text: The ant war goes on. The red ants have taken the woodpile. You have decided to write a history of the war.

effects.log: A long and serious history. The whole house reads it, and laughs, and keeps it.
General Long Legs of the Red. General Tiny of the Black. You report on them at dinner.

events.text: The ant hills are gone, under a new shed. You are surprised how much you mind.

choices.text: Hold a little funeral for the war

effects.log: You bury a twig with full honours. A neighbour's child plays a leaf like a trumpet.

choices.text: Look for the ants under the shed

effects.log: They are there. Both armies. Living under one roof. You tell everyone the war is over.

events.text: Behind a waterfall there is a cave, and when you shout into it, it shouts back, but not quite what you said.

effects.log: It answers with a name that is nearly yours. You run all the way home, delighted.
You ask what is at the back. It answers: the back. You decide that is fair.

events.text: You take your friends to the cave. Nobody believes you until the cave answers.

choices.text: Let the cave speak for itself

effects.log: Five children shouting into a cave. It answers all of them. Nobody sleeps that night.

choices.text: Go further in with a torch

ok.log: At the back, a little pool and a carved stone, very old. Somebody shouted here long before you.

fail.log: You bang your head on the low roof. The cave laughs, or echoes, or both.

events.text: Back at the waterfall, grown. The cave is still there. You are taller than the entrance now.

effects.log: It answers with your name exactly, this time. You stand there a long time.

choices.text: Bring a child to hear it

effects.log: The child shouts. The cave answers. The child grabs your hand, delighted, exactly as you did.

events.text: Summer, and the trees are full of empty cicada shells, clinging to the bark. The village herbalist says they are medicine and pays a copper for ten.

effects.log: A hundred shells, ten coppers, and a summer of climbing trees.
You keep six perfect shells in a box. They are your treasure.

events.text: The herbalist shows you what the shells are for: a fever tea. Your little cousin has a fever.

effects.log: Your six perfect shells go into the pot. The cousin is better by morning.
You climb every tree in the lane. The cousin drinks the tea, makes a face, and gets better.

events.text: The herbalist has taught you the names of thirty plants now, since the summer of the shells, and asks if you would like to learn more.

effects.log: Afternoons in the shop, the smell of roots. You could be a herbalist. You might be one, one day.

choices.text: Say no, but come back every summer

effects.log: Every summer you bring shells. The herbalist pays a copper for ten, as always.

events.text: You fold a paper boat and set it on the stream behind the village. It sails round the bend and out of sight.

choices.text: Write your name on the next one

effects.log: Ten boats, ten names. You wonder where they go.
You follow it for a mile, until it catches in reeds. You free it. It sails on without you.

events.text: A paper boat comes down the stream toward you. It has writing on it, in a child's hand: your name, and a question. Who are you?

choices.text: Send a boat back up the stream

ok.log: You walk upstream to launch it from above. Somewhere it is found.

fail.log: The boat sinks at once. You try again. And again.

choices.text: Walk up the stream to find them

effects.log: In the next village, a child with paper boats. You stare at each other, and then laugh.

events.text: Every spring now a fleet of paper boats comes down the stream from the next village, with letters on the sails.

effects.log: Twenty boats with twenty letters. The two villages become friends, child by child.
A letter on a paper sail. You keep it for the rest of your life.

events.text: A basket of fine mushrooms is for sale at the roadside, very cheap. They look a little too red.

choices.text: Buy them and ask the herbalist

effects.log: The herbalist laughs and throws half away. The other half is delicious.
Wise. A week later a whole inn is sick from mushrooms. Not you.

events.text: A cook at the inn is about to put red mushrooms in the soup, the same red as the basket by the path.

effects.log: The cook argues. You win. The soup is plain and nobody is ill.
You eat noodles across the road. The inn is closed the next day. You were right.

events.text: The roadside basket again. This time the seller is a child, and the mushrooms are the red ones, and the child has no idea.

effects.log: You sort the basket together. The child sells only the good ones, and sells out.

choices.text: Buy the whole basket and bury it (1 tael)

effects.log: You paid 1 tael. The child is pleased. The red mushrooms go in a deep hole.

events.text: A big dog with a wild eye is loose in the lane, snarling, and children are playing at the end of it.

choices.text: Get between the dog and the children

ok.log: You face it down with a pole. It turns and runs into the fields.

fail.log: It bites your arm and runs. The children are safe. Your arm aches all winter.

effects.log: Doors slam all down the lane. The dog wanders off. Nobody is hurt.

events.text: The wild dog is back, but it is thin and limping now, and lies in your yard, not snarling.

effects.log: It eats and sleeps. In the morning it is still there.
The dog-catcher takes it away, gently. You watch it go.

events.text: The dog has lived in your yard for three years. It is the gentlest dog in the lane. A thief tried your gate last night. The thief has not been seen since.

choices.text: Give the dog the best bone in the house

effects.log: It buries it. Then digs it up. Then buries it, closer to you.

choices.text: Make it a kennel by the gate

effects.log: It ignores the kennel and sleeps across your doorstep, as always.

events.text: Winter, and the river is frozen, and the short way to market is straight across it. The ice creaks.

ok.log: You cross. The ice creaks the whole way. On the far side you breathe again.

fail.log: One foot goes through. You haul yourself out and run to market, steaming.

choices.text: Go the long way by the bridge

effects.log: Two hours longer. You arrive late and dry.

events.text: The river ice again. A cart has gone through near the bank, the mule kicking, the carter shouting.

choices.text: Lay planks and pull the mule out

ok.log: Planks, ropes and three helpers. The mule comes out, steaming. The carter cries.

fail.log: You go through the ice too. Everyone gets out, cold and furious.

effects.log: The whole village comes with ropes. The mule and the carter are saved. You get a hot meal.

events.text: A winter so cold the river ice is thick enough for a fair. Stalls, skating, roast chestnuts. It is the first ice fair in fifty years.

ok.log: You skate badly and then well. A child follows you, holding your sleeve.

fail.log: You fall twenty times. Everyone does. It is the best fair in fifty years.

choices.text: Sell hot tea on the ice

effects.log: You sell out in an hour. Your hands are frozen. Your purse is warm.

events.text: A horse has bolted in the market, dragging an empty cart, straight toward the fruit stalls.

ok.log: You hang on, and are dragged ten yards, and the horse stops. The fruit sellers cheer.

fail.log: You are dragged into the oranges. The horse stops there anyway. You smell of oranges for a week.

effects.log: You shout and push people aside. The horse runs through the gap and stops in the river, calmly.

events.text: The horse's owner, a farmer, has found you to say thank you, and has brought the horse, which seems to remember you.

effects.log: The horse watches you eat one. You give the horse one too.

ok.log: A month of work. The horse never bolts again.

fail.log: The horse throws you twice. The third week, it lets you ride.

events.text: The market is busy, and a cart horse is skittish, and everyone looks at you.

ok.log: You speak to it quietly. It stops. You have a reputation now.

fail.log: It does not calm. The owner leads it away. Everyone says you tried.

choices.text: Hold the bridle until it settles

effects.log: A long minute. It settles. The market breathes.

events.text: Smoke pours out of your stove the wrong way and the kitchen fills: the chimney is blocked.

ok.log: A bird's nest, abandoned, and a great deal of soot. You come down black.

fail.log: You slip on the roof. You clear it anyway, from the edge. Your elbow is not happy.

choices.text: Put out the stove and send for a sweep (1 tael)

effects.log: You paid 1 tael. The sweep is a small, silent person who is up and down in a minute.

events.text: Smoke from a neighbour's roof, black and thick, and a crackling sound: the neighbour's chimney is on fire.

choices.text: Climb up with a wet sack

ok.log: You smother the chimney. The fire dies. The neighbour brings you dinner for a month.

fail.log: You burn your hands, but the fire dies. The neighbour brings you dinner for a month anyway.

effects.log: The lane comes running. The fire is out in minutes. Nobody is hurt.

events.text: You have become the person the lane calls when a chimney smokes. Today it is the temple's.

effects.log: A whole nest of swallows. You move it to the eaves. The monks say you have earned merit.

choices.text: Teach the young monks to sweep it

effects.log: They are terrible at first. By the end, one of them is better than you.

events.text: A wasps' nest the size of a melon has appeared under your eaves, and the wasps are cross about everything.

ok.log: Damp straw, a long pole, and a slow retreat. The nest is empty by morning.

fail.log: They are not as sleepy as you hoped. You run. They follow. You jump in the water butt.

effects.log: You use the back door all summer. In winter the nest is empty and very beautiful.

events.text: A wasp nest under the eaves again. This time you know a trick: a paper bag, a fast hand, and a long run.

ok.log: The nest is in the bag and the bag is in the river. You are not stung once.

fail.log: The bag tears. You run, and you remember why last time you waited.

effects.log: You use the back door again. The nest, in winter, goes on your shelf beside the last one.

events.text: You have a shelf of empty wasp nests now, each one a summer. A child from the lane asks why you keep them.

choices.text: Tell the story of each one

effects.log: The child laughs at the water butt, and gasps at the bag, and goes home to tell everyone.
The child carries it home like treasure. The next summer, the child's family has a nest too.

events.text: After a week of rain the mountain road is half gone, a slope of mud, and the next town is on the other side.

ok.log: You cross. Behind you, a little more of the road slides away.

fail.log: You slide halfway down and climb back up, caked. The road wins today.

effects.log: A day at the roadside shrine. The next morning, the road crew is there.

events.text: The mountain road again. A merchant's family is stuck on the far side of a new slide, with a sick child.

ok.log: One by one, step by step. The child is carried by you. Everyone crosses.

fail.log: You fall once, carrying the child. Neither of you is hurt. Everyone crosses, muddy.

choices.text: Go back for the road crew

effects.log: The crew come with planks. The family crosses on a bridge of boards.

events.text: The mountain road has been rebuilt with a stone wall. The road crew, who remember you, ask you to lay the last stone.

effects.log: The last stone of the wall. You press it into place. It will be there a hundred years.

choices.text: Carve a warning on it for the rains

effects.log: Wait a day, it says. Travellers read it for a hundred years.

events.arc: The Night the Roof Came In
events.text: A storm in the night, and a beam of your roof cracks, and rain pours in over your bed.

choices.text: Prop the beam with a post

ok.log: You hold the post with your back until it is wedged. The roof holds till morning.

fail.log: The beam comes down beside you. You sleep under the table, wet.

choices.text: Move everything to the dry corner

effects.log: You sleep in a corner with all your belongings piled round you. It is a sort of fort.

events.arc: The Night the Roof Came In
events.text: The roof is mended, but now every storm you lie awake listening to the beams.

choices.text: Learn the sounds of the beams

effects.log: You learn which creak is fine and which is not. After that, you sleep through storms.

choices.text: Ask a carpenter to check every beam (2 taels)

effects.log: You paid 2 taels. The carpenter finds two more cracked. You sleep very well.

events.arc: The Night the Roof Came In
events.text: A storm, and the neighbour's roof comes in, and the neighbour's family is standing in your doorway, soaked.

effects.log: Five people in your dry corner. The storm passes. The family talks about that night for years.

ok.log: You know exactly where to put the post. The roof holds.

fail.log: The post slips. The family moves in with you for the night.

events.text: At the fair, a light hand slides into your sleeve and out again, and your purse goes with it.

ok.log: You catch the thief at the noodle stall. It is a child. You get the purse back and buy the child noodles.

fail.log: You trip over a goose. The thief is gone. The goose is offended.

choices.text: Let it go and shout a warning

effects.log: The whole fair checks its sleeves. Nobody else is robbed that day.

events.text: The fair again. You see the same light hand reaching into an old woman's sleeve.

ok.log: You catch the wrist. It is the same child, grown. You do not call the watch. You talk.

fail.log: You miss. The old woman feels it and slaps the child. You both laugh, later.

effects.log: She holds her sleeve tight. The child looks at you, and you look back.

events.text: At the fair a young stall-keeper waves you over and gives you a bowl of noodles for nothing: the child with the light hands, grown, honest.

effects.log: They are very good noodles. You pay for the second bowl, and get a nod.

choices.text: Ask how the stall came about

effects.log: A bowl of noodles at a fair, years ago, and a talk. You do not remember saying anything wise. The stall-keeper does.

events.text: Your mother, {npc}, holds out a hand from across the courtyard. The old midwife holds you up by the arms. Everyone is waiting for you to walk.

effects.log: Six steps, then a sit. The courtyard cheers. The old midwife claims the credit.
You walk eight steps, after a chicken. Nobody can decide if it counts.

events.text: You can walk now, and you use it mainly to escape. Today you have reached the gate.

effects.log: You get as far as the neighbour's dog, which licks your face. You are carried home in triumph.
You stand in the gate and wave at everyone. Your mother, {npc}, laughs and says you will be a magistrate.

events.text: Your parents measure you against the doorpost every New Year. This year you have grown a whole hand.

effects.log: Your father, {npc}, marks the post. You stand on your toes. {He} marks it anyway.
You stand on a stool to mark {his} height. {He} is very tall, you announce. Everyone agrees.

events.arc: The Morning of the Big Word
events.text: You have been saying ba and ma for weeks. This morning you look at the family dog and say something new.

effects.log: Your first real word, and it is for the dog. The dog is very proud. Your parents pretend not to mind.
Your first word is rice. Your mother, {npc}, says you will never go hungry.

events.arc: The Morning of the Big Word
events.text: You have learned the word no, and use it for everything.

effects.log: You lose. You are bathed. You say no throughout.
You stay up an hour and fall asleep on the dog. Your father, {npc}, carries you both in.

events.arc: The Morning of the Big Word
events.text: The old midwife teaches you a song with forty verses. You remember all of them, and sing them at dinner, every night.

effects.log: Forty verses. The whole house knows them now too, whether they wanted to or not.
Your verse is about the dog. The old midwife adds it to the song.

events.text: Your cradle is by the window, and the moon looks in every night. You reach for it.

effects.log: You cannot reach it. You reach every night anyway. Your mother, {npc}, says you will reach a great deal.
You sleep through the night for the first time. The moon is thanked, formally, by the old midwife.

events.text: The cradle is too small now. Your father, {npc}, makes you a little bed and puts it by the same window.

effects.log: The bed stays by the window. The moon looks in. You are satisfied.

choices.text: Ask for the dog in the bed

effects.log: The dog is allowed one night. It stays for years.

events.text: Your mother, {npc}, tells you the story of the rabbit in the moon, who pounds medicine all night for the sick.

choices.text: Ask to be a doctor like the rabbit

effects.log: Your mother says you can be anything. You choose rabbit. {He} says that is fine.

choices.text: Stay up to see the rabbit

effects.log: You see a shape. It might be a rabbit. You fall asleep before it moves.

events.text: The old midwife ties a red thread round your wrist against bad luck. You try to eat it immediately.

effects.log: The old midwife ties another, higher up. You try to eat that too.
The thread stays on all year. The old midwife is very pleased with your wisdom.

events.text: You fall in the pond and come out laughing. The old midwife says it was the thread, and ties another one.

effects.log: The old midwife ties a third thread. You are now very lucky and very wet.
You watch the pond from a distance. The old midwife is relieved.

events.text: The old midwife ties a red thread on the newest baby in the family, and asks you to help.

effects.log: Your knot is bad. The old midwife leaves it, for luck.

choices.text: Tell the baby about the pond

effects.log: The baby listens to the pond story with great attention, or sleeps. It is hard to tell.

events.text: A peddler sells your parents a little rattle drum. You discover that if you twist it, it makes a noise, forever.

effects.log: You twist it until your father, {npc}, hides it in the rice jar. You find it.
The dog takes the drum and buries it. A week later you dig it up.

events.text: The drum has broken, and you are inconsolable, and your father, {npc}, is trying to mend it.

effects.log: You hold the string. Your father ties it. The drum is noisier than ever.
Your father says when you are older. You remind {him} every day.

events.text: The village holds a parade, and you are allowed to march at the end with the little drum.

effects.log: You drum all the way round the village, out of time. Everyone claps.
The big drummer lets you hit the big drum once. It is the best moment of your life so far.

events.text: A stray cat has started sleeping beside your cradle. Your mother, {npc}, tried to shoo it away. It came back.

effects.log: The cat lets you, once. Then it moves to the foot of the cradle.
The cat looks at you as if you are very stupid, and stays.

events.text: The cat brings you a gift: a mouse, not dead, which escapes into the kitchen.

effects.log: You, the cat and your mother, {npc}, chase the mouse round the kitchen. The mouse wins.
The cat eats your dumpling. Your mother gives you another, and gives the cat a look.

events.text: The cat is old and slow now, and sleeps in your lap in the sun.

effects.log: You sit still for a whole afternoon. Your mother, {npc}, has never seen it before.
The cat sleeps through your story. You decide it liked it.

events.text: The first rain you remember: you stand in the doorway with your hand out, and the rain lands on it.

effects.log: You run round the courtyard, laughing, soaked. Your mother, {npc}, runs after you, laughing too.
A whole bowl of rain. You carry it indoors to show the household. Most of it arrives.

events.text: A great puddle in the lane after the rain. The biggest puddle you have ever seen.

effects.log: The biggest splash in the lane. A neighbour is splashed. The neighbour laughs.
Your leaf crosses the whole puddle. You declare it a ship.

events.text: Rain again, and this time you stand in the doorway with your little cousin, holding out both your hands.

choices.text: Show the cousin how to run in it

effects.log: Two small children, soaked and shrieking. Two parents, laughing in the doorway.

choices.text: Catch the rain in a bowl for the cousin

effects.log: The cousin drinks the rain. You are both amazed it tastes of nothing.

events.text: First snow, and your rival {npc} gets you with a snowball before you are out of the gate.

choices.text: Build a fort and fight back

ok.log: Your fort holds. {npc} surrenders with a white flag, which is a snowball on a stick.

fail.log: {npc}'s fort is better. You are buried. You laugh anyway.

choices.text: Call a truce and build a snow lion together

mem.note: built a snow lion with me

effects.log: The best snow lion in the lane. It lasts a week. You both visit it daily.

events.text: First snow again, and you are waiting at the gate with a snowball. So, you can see from across the lane, is {npc}.

ok.log: Got. {npc} throws back. The whole lane joins in.

fail.log: {npc} is faster. Got. The lane joins in anyway.

effects.log: {npc} waves back, suspicious, and then drops {his} snowball too.

events.text: First snow, years on. You find a small snow lion on your doorstep in the morning.

effects.log: The next morning there are two on yours.
{npc} opens the window, laughing, and throws one back.

events.text: The old orchard's best apple tree hangs over the wall, and your rival {npc} has claimed it, and stands under it like a guard.

choices.text: Climb the other side and pick first

ok.log: You pick the reddest one. {npc} sees and chases you three streets.

fail.log: {npc} catches your ankle. You both fall in the nettles.

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it for a long time and gives you the second-best apple.

events.text: The orchard owner has caught {npc} in the apple tree and is marching {him} home by the ear.

choices.text: Tell the owner it was you too

effects.log: The owner marches you both home. {npc} looks at you sideways all the way.
{npc} sees you laughing and does not forget it for a year.

events.text: The orchard is for sale. You and {npc} have both come to look at it, separately, and meet under the apple tree.

effects.log: You paid 4 taels each. The tree is yours, both. The apples are shared, mostly fairly.

choices.text: Pick one apple each and leave it for the next children

mem.note: left the tree for the children

effects.log: You walk away together. You hear children at the wall behind you.

events.text: The village races little lantern boats down the stream at the festival, and your rival {npc} has won three years running with a boat shaped like a duck.

choices.text: Build a boat shaped like a swan

ok.log: Your swan wins. {npc} studies it for an hour afterwards.

fail.log: The swan capsizes. The duck wins. {npc} is magnanimous, which is worse.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how the duck is built

effects.log: {npc} explains, suspicious, then proud. Your boat next year is also a duck.

events.text: The festival again. Your boat and {npc}'s are stuck together in the reeds at the first bend.

effects.log: Both boats come in last, together. The village cheers the two of you.
Yours finishes. {npc}'s burns in the reeds. {npc} says nothing.

events.text: {npc} has made a lantern boat for a child of your street, and hands it over with great ceremony.

effects.log: The boat is shaped like a duck. It wins. {npc} cheers louder than anyone.

choices.text: Build one for {npc}'s side of the street

mem.note: built a boat for my street

effects.log: Swan and duck, side by side. The children race them. Nobody keeps score.

events.text: The academy holds a public debate, and you and your rival {npc} are on opposite sides of the question of whether rain is good for rice.

ok.log: You win. {npc} says you won on a technicality: that rain is wet.

fail.log: {npc} wins with a poem about drought. You applaud, very reluctantly.

choices.text: Argue that the question is silly

effects.log: The audience agrees with you. The examiners do not. {npc} laughs, despite {him}self.

events.text: A real drought, and the county needs someone to argue its case for relief at the provincial court. The magistrate names you and {npc} together.

effects.log: You argue about every line. The petition is perfect. The relief comes.

ok.log: Your half is better. The relief comes. {npc} says so first.

fail.log: {npc}'s half is better. The relief comes. You say so first.

events.text: The rains have come back, and the rice is good, and the academy has asked you and {npc} to debate the old question again.

effects.log: {npc} loses on purpose, beautifully. The audience knows. Everyone laughs.
You argue against rain. {npc} argues for it. You are both brilliant. It is a draw.

events.text: Every spring the young people of the valley race up the sacred peak. Your rival {npc} has won twice.

ok.log: You reach the top first. {npc} arrives a moment later and sits down beside you without a word.

fail.log: {npc} wins again. At the top {npc} hands you water.

effects.log: You reach the top together. The judges cannot decide. You share the prize, a jar of honey.

events.text: The peak race, and halfway up {npc} has twisted an ankle in the rocks.

effects.log: You come in last, together. The valley talks about it more than any win.

choices.text: Race on and send help back

effects.log: You win. Help reaches {npc} in an hour. {npc} congratulates you, through gritted teeth.

events.text: You are both too old for the race now, and both judges at the top of the peak, waiting for the young ones.

choices.text: Back a favourite with the honey

effects.log: Neither of you picks the winner. You share the honey anyway.

choices.text: Tell the young ones about your races
